script.first: Count by tens from 10 to 100 aloud together. Find the orange dot at 10 together. Ask, "What comes after 10 when we count by tens?" Draw the first line together. The row of numbers at the bottom of the page shows the order.
script.stuck: Have the child say the number they are on and add ten; that is the dot to look for. The numbers in the row at the bottom can be crossed off one by one.

packs.title: Second Grade Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Second Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the start of the year in second grade: 8 review blocks in reading, word work, writing, and math, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: 10 More, 10 Less
blocks.instruction: Write the number that is 10 less and the number that is 10 more.

script.say: "Look at the number in the middle. On the left, write the number that is 10 less. On the right, write the number that is 10 more."
script.first: Do the first one on the board. Ask: "Ten more than 36. Which digit changes, the tens or the ones?" Show that only the tens digit changes: 26, 36, 46. Count by tens from another number together, for example 7, 17, 27, 37.
script.stuck: If the classroom has a hundreds chart, have the child find the number on it: the number straight above is 10 less, and the number straight below is 10 more. Without a chart, have the child cover the ones digit and change the tens digit by one.

blocks.title: Fill in the Blank: Choose the Word
blocks.instruction: Look at the picture and read the sentence. Circle the word that fits and write it in the box.

script.say: "Each sentence has a gap, and under it are two words. Look at the picture and read the sentence. Circle the word that fits, and write it in the box."
script.first: Do the first sentence together. Read it aloud and say "blank" at the gap. Read the two words under it. Try each one in the sentence and ask, "Does that make sense? Does it match the picture?" Circle the right word and write it in the box.
script.stuck: Read the sentence with the child, one word at a time, and have the child say it once with each of the two words. The picture next to the sentence shows which one is meant.

blocks.title: Fill in the Blank: Plural Nouns
blocks.instruction: Look at the pictures. There is more than one. Write the word for more than one in the box.

script.say: "Look at the pictures in each row. There is more than one. Write the word for more than one in the box, so that the sentence is complete."
script.first: Do the first sentence together. Ask: "What are these? One cow, three…?" Write the word on the board and point to the s at the end. Read the whole sentence aloud. The children do the other sentences the same way.
script.stuck: Ask the child to name one of the pictures, then say "one ___, two ___" aloud. A careful spelling that you can read is enough. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the pictures are cows, lions, hens, planes, penguins, monkeys, balls, and bats; other words that fit the picture, such as chickens or airplanes, are right as well.

blocks.title: Rewrite the Sentence with a Pronoun
blocks.instruction: Read the sentence. Write it again on the lines, but use a pronoun instead of the name.

script.say: "We do not say a name over and over. We use a short word in its place: he, she, or they. Read each sentence. Then write it again on the lines with he, she, or they in place of the name or names."
script.first: Do the first sentence on the board: "Ben rides a bike." Ask, "Who is the sentence about? One boy, one girl, or more than one person?" Write the new sentence: "He rides a bike." Point out the capital letter at the start and the period at the end.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger under the name or names and ask whether it is one person or more than one, and a boy or a girl. Two names joined by "and" become "They." The rest of the sentence is copied word for word. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the new sentences start with He, They, They, They, He, She, He, and She.

blocks.title: Where on the Number Line? 40 to 60
blocks.instruction: This line does not start at zero. Count on from the nearest label.

script.say: "These number lines do not start at zero. They start at 40 and go to 60. Each arrow points to a number. Find out which number it is and write it in the box."
script.first: Draw the first number line on the board. Read the printed numbers aloud: 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. Ask, "How much is one small step?" (One.) Find the printed number closest to the first arrow and count on or back from it to the arrow.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the nearest printed number and count the small marks one by one to the arrow, saying the numbers: "50, 51, 52, 53." An answer such as 3 means the child wrote the number of steps and not the number on the line. An answer such as 13 means the child counted from the left end as if it were zero; point to the 40. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the arrows point to 53 and 57 on the first line, 42 and 48 on the second, and 41 and 54 on the third.

blocks.title: Subtraction Practice to 20
blocks.instruction: Solve each problem in your head. Write the missing number in the box.

script.say: "This is math you already know: subtracting with numbers up to 20. Do the ones you know first. Then go back to the others."
script.first: Do the first two problems on the board. Ask how the children got their answers and accept every way that gives the right answer: counting back, counting up from the smaller number, or just knowing it.
script.stuck: Have the child count up from the smaller number to the bigger one on fingers: for 17 minus 9, say "9" and count up to 17. Drawing dots and crossing them out is fine, too. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 4, 12, 2, 8, 8, 8, 5, 2, 10, 5, 3, and 4.

blocks.title: Whose Kite Is It?
blocks.instruction: Follow each string from an animal to its kite or balloon. Write the animal's number in the box above it.

script.say: "Four animals are flying kites and a balloon, and the strings are tangled. Follow each string from the animal up to its kite or balloon. Then write the animal's number in the box above it."
script.first: Hold up the page and put your finger on animal number 1. Follow its string slowly with your finger, straight through each crossing, up to the top. Write a 1 in the box above that kite. The children do the other three.
script.stuck: Have the child trace the string with a finger first and then with a colored pencil, one color for each animal. At a crossing the string goes straight on; it does not turn onto the other string.

blocks.title: Beginning, Middle and End of a Story
blocks.instruction: Look at the beginning and the end of each story and draw what happens in the middle frame.

script.say: "Each story on this page has a beginning and an end, but the middle is missing. Look at what is different between the first picture and the last one. Then draw what happens in the middle."
script.first: Do the first story together by talking, not drawing. Ask a child to say what the first picture shows and another child what the last picture shows. Ask: "What must have happened in between?" Take two or three ideas. Then each child draws the middle picture.
script.stuck: Ask the child: "What is here at the beginning? What is different at the end? What did someone do to make that happen?" Any drawing that leads from the first picture to the last is right; it does not have to be neat.

packs.title: Second Grade Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaTitle: Second Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the middle of the year in second grade: 8 review blocks in reading, word work, writing, and math, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Read the Calendar: A First Look
blocks.instruction: Look at the month. Answer each question by reading the calendar.

script.say: "This is a calendar page for one month. The questions under it ask you to find things on the calendar. Read each question and write the answer in the box."
script.first: Read the name of the month and the names of the days across the top together. Do the first question together: find the date, put a finger on it, and go straight up to the name of the day. Write the answer. Read the other questions aloud once before the children start.
script.stuck: For a question about a day of the week, have the child find the day's name at the top and move a finger straight down its column. For a question about a picture, the child looks for the little picture inside the calendar. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are Thursday, 4, the 21st, and 31.

blocks.title: Who Am I? Mystery Animal
blocks.instruction: Read the five clues on each card. Find the animal in the picture bank, write its name on the line and draw it in the box.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Each card has five clues about a mystery animal. Read all five clues. Then find the animal in the picture bank at the top, write its name on the line, and draw it in the box."
script.first: Name the six animals in the picture bank together. Read the first card aloud. After each clue ask, "Which animals can it still be?" and let the children rule animals out: it has fur, so it is not the lizard, the ant, or the eagle; it cannot fly, so it is not the bat. Tell the children that one clue is never enough; all five clues have to fit.
script.stuck: Have the child read one clue at a time and put a finger on every animal in the bank that fits it, lifting a finger each time a clue rules an animal out. A quick sketch in the box is enough. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the animals are the bear (the wolf does not eat plants), the ant, and the eagle.

blocks.title: Synonyms: Circle the Word That Means the Same
blocks.instruction: Read the big word on each card and circle the word under it that means the same.

script.say: "Synonyms are words that mean the same thing, or almost the same, like big and large. Read the big word on each card. Then circle the word under it that means the same."
script.first: Do the first card together. Read the big word and the four words under it aloud. Try each one in a sentence: "The room was quiet. The room was sleepy? The room was hushed?" Circle the one that keeps the meaning. Read the words of the other cards aloud once, because some of them are new to second graders.
script.stuck: Read the words of the card to the child and have the child put each one into the same short sentence. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are quiet and hushed, shut and close, yell and shout, jump and leap, amazed and astonished, noisy and loud, peaceful and calm, grumpy and angry.

blocks.title: Write the Question
blocks.instruction: Read the answer. Look at the highlighted words. Write the question that asks for them on the line.

script.say: "Each sentence on this page is an answer. Some of its words are highlighted. Write the question that asks for those words. Start with a question word: who, what, where, when, or how many."
script.first: Do the first and the third on the board. Read the first sentence and point to the highlighted word: "Mia finds four balls." Ask, "Is Mia a person, a thing, a place, or a time?" A person, so the question starts with Who: "Who finds four balls?" In the third sentence, "in the kitchen" is highlighted. That is a place, so the question starts with Where: "Where is Zoe?" Write both questions with a capital letter and a question mark.
script.stuck: Ask what the highlighted words tell: a person (who), a thing or an animal (what), a place (where), a time (when), or a number (how many). Then help the child say the question aloud before writing it. For your own reference, good questions for the page for everyone are: Who finds four balls? Who eats at two o'clock? Where is Zoe? When does Anna sleep? How many kiwis does Leo see? What does Emma like? What does Ava draw? Where does Ben play? Another wording that asks for the highlighted words is right, too.

blocks.title: 2-Digit Column Addition
blocks.instruction: Add one place at a time. Start with the ones.

script.say: "These addition problems are written one number under the other. Add one place at a time. Start on the right with the ones. Then add the tens."
script.first: Write the first problem on the board the way it is printed. Add the ones and write the answer under the ones. Add the tens and write the answer under the tens. Read the whole answer aloud. None of the problems on the page for everyone needs regrouping.
script.stuck: Have the child cover the tens column with a finger and add only the ones, then cover the ones and add the tens. Fingers or dots are fine for the small sums. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 35, 84, 67, 92, 89, and 89.

blocks.title: Shopping Math: Add Up the Basket
blocks.instruction: Every card asks for a total. Add the prices together.

script.say: "At the top of the page is a shelf with five toys and their prices. Each question tells you what someone buys. Find the prices on the shelf, add them, and write the total."
script.first: Read the five prices on the shelf aloud together. Do the first question together: find the two things on the shelf, write their prices in the work space, and add them. Write the total in the box in front of the cent sign.
script.stuck: Have the child circle the two things on the shelf that the question shows, then write the two prices one under the other and add the ones first. Coins or drawn dimes and pennies help a child who cannot add the numbers yet.

blocks.title: Logic Grid Puzzles: Three Clues, One Answer
blocks.instruction: Read the clues. Cross out on the grid what cannot be true, check what must be true, then circle the picture each child has.

script.say: "These are logic puzzles. In each puzzle three children each have one of the three pictures at the top of the grid, and no two children have the same one. The clues tell you what a child does NOT have. Put an X in the grid for every clue. When only one box is left in a row, that is what the child has."
script.first: Do the first puzzle together. Read the first clue aloud, find the child's row and the picture's column, and put an X in the box where they meet. Do the other two clues the same way. Then show the two rules: a row with two Xs gets a check mark in its last box, and a check mark puts an X in every other box of its row and its column, because each child has only one picture and only one child has each picture. The small grid at the top right of the page shows this: one check mark with Xs around it. When every row has a check mark, find each child's strip under the puzzle and circle the picture that child has. Children do the second puzzle on their own. Children who finish write one sentence for each child on the back ("Ben has the dog."), then make up a puzzle for a partner: three names, three pictures, and three "does not have" clues.
script.stuck: Have the child read one clue at a time and make its X before reading the next one. Then ask, "Which row has only one empty box? Which column?" A box that is the last one left in its row or in its column gets the check mark. For your own reference, on the page for everyone: in the first puzzle Ben has the dog, Mia the mouse, and Tom the cat; in the second puzzle Leo has the frog, Max the hamster, and Emma the turtle.

blocks.title: Help the Rabbit Pick Up Every Carrot
blocks.instruction: Help the rabbit get to the bucket and pick up every carrot, without using a path twice. Tick a circle for each carrot.

script.say: "The rabbit wants to get to the bucket and pick up every carrot on the way. There is one rule: the rabbit may not use the same path twice. Check a circle each time you pick up a carrot."
script.first: Hold up the page and show the rabbit, the bucket, and the four carrots. Tell the children to plan the whole way with a finger before they draw, because the first way they see may miss a carrot. The printed directions say "tick a circle"; tell the children that means a check mark.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on each carrot first and look at which paths lead to it. If the way is blocked because a path was already used, the child starts again with a finger and tries the carrots in another order.

packs.title: Second Grade Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Second Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the middle of the year in second grade: 8 review blocks in reading, word work, writing, and math, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Number Walls with Two-Digit Answers
blocks.instruction: The bricks climb past twenty, so add in writing as you go.

script.say: "This is a number wall. Each brick is the sum of the two bricks right under it. Start at the bottom and build every wall to the top. The numbers get bigger than twenty, so you may add on paper."
script.first: Draw the first wall on the board. Point to two bricks that sit side by side in the bottom row and to the brick that rests on both of them. Add them and write the sum in that brick. Fill in the second row together, then let the children finish the wall.
script.stuck: Put two fingers on the two bricks under the empty brick and have the child add those two numbers on scrap paper, tens and ones. A wrong brick lower down makes every brick above it wrong, so check the rows from the bottom up. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the top bricks of the four walls are 60, 70, 46, and 49.

blocks.title: Family Relationships: Riddles
blocks.instruction: Read each riddle and write the right family word from the box on the line; one word can fit more than one riddle.

script.say: "Now it is time to read and think. Each sentence is a riddle about Tom's family. Read the riddle and work it out step by step. Then write the right family word from the box on the line. You will use each word more than one time."
script.first: Read the four words in the box aloud together. Do the first riddle on the board in two steps, drawing a stick person for each step: "Tom's dad's mom. Start with Tom. Step one: Tom's dad. Step two: his dad's mom. What does Tom call his dad's mom?" Write grandma. Keep every example about Tom's family, not about the children's own families. Tell the children that some families use other names, such as Nana or Abuela; on this page they use the words in the box.
script.stuck: Have the child cover the end of the riddle and say who the first two words are ("Tom's mom"), then add the last word ("her brother"). A quick sketch of three stick people helps. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are grandma, uncle, grandma, aunt, grandpa, aunt, grandpa, and uncle.

blocks.title: Split the Compound: Find the Two Words
blocks.instruction: The whole word is printed letter by letter next to its picture. Draw one line where the second word starts.

script.say: "A compound word is made of two smaller words, like sun and flower in sunflower. Each word on this page is printed letter by letter. Draw one line where the second word starts."
script.first: Write "bluebell" on the board with spaces between the letters. Ask, "Which two words do you hear?" Draw a line between blue and bell. Have the children say both words. They do the other words the same way.
script.stuck: Have the child say the whole word and clap once for each of the two small words, then cover the end of the word with a finger and move it until a real word shows. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are blue-bell, book-shelf, sand-castle, scare-crow, rain-bow, butter-cup, key-board, and earth-worm.

blocks.title: Verb Forms in Sentences with Pictures
blocks.instruction: Look at the picture and read the verb in the chip. Write the form that fits the sentence in the dashed box.

script.say: "Each sentence has a gap, and the verb for the gap is in the little chip at the end. Write the verb in the form that fits the sentence. Sometimes it needs an s. Sometimes it happened yesterday and needs a different ending."
script.first: Do two on the board. Read the third sentence with the verb as it is printed: "On Mondays Anna sing at the club." Ask, "Does that sound right?" Fix it: "On Mondays Anna sings at the club." Then do the fifth sentence the same way: "Tom jump at the pool yesterday" becomes "Tom jumped at the pool yesterday." Tell the children to look for words like today, every day, and yesterday.
script.stuck: Have the child read the sentence aloud with the verb and listen. If the sentence has "yesterday," the verb tells about the past (jumped). With one person and "today" or "every day," the verb gets an s (runs, sings). For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are reads, runs, sings, wanders, jumped, and dances. In the first, second, and last sentences a form for the past (read, ran, danced) also makes a correct sentence; count it as right.

blocks.title: Measure It!
blocks.instruction: Each object starts at 0. Read the ruler and write how many units long it is.

script.say: "Each shape sits on a ruler and starts at 0. Read the ruler at the end of the shape and write how many units long the shape is."
script.first: Do the first one together. Put a finger on the 0, where the shape starts, and slide it to the place where the shape ends. Read the number there and write it in the box. Say the answer with the unit: "It is 3 units long."
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the right end of the shape and move it straight down to the ruler. The number under the finger is the length. A child who counts the marks gets one too many; count the spaces between the marks instead.

blocks.title: Expanded Form Both Ways
blocks.instruction: Put the parts together, or break each number into hundreds, tens and ones. Write the numbers in the boxes.

script.say: "Every digit in a number is worth something. In 479, the 4 is worth 400, the 7 is worth 70, and the 9 is worth 9. This page goes both ways. When the parts are printed, put them together and write the number in the box. When the number is printed, break it into its hundreds, its tens, and its ones."
script.first: Write 400 + 70 + 9 = on the board, as in problem 1. Ask, "How many hundreds? How many tens? How many ones?" and write 479. Then write 756 = with three empty boxes, as in problem 5. Read it aloud, "seven hundred fifty-six," and ask what each digit is worth: 700 + 50 + 6. Point to the 5 and say, "This 5 stands for 50, so 50 goes in the middle box." The easier page has only tens and ones; give it to everyone if the class has not worked with hundreds yet. On the page for early finishers, the parts are out of order and a place can be missing: 50 + 600 is 650.
script.stuck: Have the child read the number aloud slowly and write what each part says: "two hundred" is 200, "forty" is 40, "two" is 2. A child who writes 2 + 4 + 2 for 242 has copied the digits; point to the first 2 and ask, "Is this 2 ones or 2 hundreds?" The usual order is hundreds, tens, ones; the right three parts in another order, such as 40 + 200 + 2, are still correct. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are, in the order of the problems, 479, 988, 926, 798, 700 + 50 + 6, 771, 200 + 40 + 2, 200 + 20 + 9, 800 + 40 + 5, and 800 + 30 + 3.

blocks.title: Picture Sudoku
blocks.instruction: Every row, column, and box needs all four pictures — draw or write what goes in each empty cell.

script.say: "This is a picture puzzle. Each row across, each column down, and each small box needs all four pictures, one of each. Find out which picture is missing in each empty space, and draw it or write its first letter."
script.first: Do one empty space together. Pick a row that has only one empty space and name the three pictures that are already in it. Ask, "Which one is missing?" Draw it in. Tell the children to always look for the row, column, or box that is almost full.
script.stuck: Point to a row or column with only one empty space and have the child name the pictures in it. If none is that full, have the child check the row and the column of one empty space together to see which pictures are already used.

blocks.title: Count by 5s to the Rainbow
blocks.instruction: Help the balloon float to the rainbow. Count by 5s from cloud to cloud, all the way to 100.

script.say: "The balloon wants to float up to the rainbow. It can only go from cloud to cloud by counting by fives: 5, 10, 15, and so on, all the way to 100. Draw its way."
script.first: Count by fives to 100 aloud together. Find the balloon and the cloud with the 5 together. Ask, "Which cloud comes next?" Draw the line to 10 together. Tell the children that some clouds are traps: a number can be on the page more than once, and only the one next to the path counts.
script.stuck: Have the child say the number they are on and add five, then look only at the clouds that touch the path from where they are. If the path ends, the child goes back to the last cloud and looks for the same number somewhere else.

packs.title: Second Grade Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaTitle: Second Grade Emergency Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the end of the year in second grade: 8 review blocks in reading, word work, writing, and math, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: 100 More, 100 Less
blocks.instruction: Write the number that is 100 less and the number that is 100 more.

script.say: "Look at the number in the middle. On the left, write the number that is 100 less. On the right, write the number that is 100 more."
script.first: Do the first one on the board. Ask: "A hundred more. Which digit changes? Which two stay the same?" Show that only the hundreds digit changes: 249, 349, 449. Count by hundreds from another number together.
script.stuck: Have the child cover the tens and the ones with a finger and look only at the hundreds digit: one less for 100 less, one more for 100 more. The two covered digits are copied as they are.

blocks.title: Read and Answer
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. Then read each question and circle the best answer. The answers are in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, find the sentence in the story that answers it, and circle the answer. The children do the other questions on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask them to put a finger on the sentence in the story that tells the answer. If the child cannot read the story alone, read it with them. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are her grandpa, a rabbit, and in the evening.

blocks.title: Find the Root Word
blocks.instruction: Circle the part the three words share and write that root word in the empty stone.

script.say: "The three words on each card are a word family: they are all built from one small word, the root word. Circle the part that all three words share. Then write the root word in the empty stone."
script.first: Look at the first card together; it is already done. Read the three words and the root word: cheerful, cheerfully, cheerily, cheer. Do the second card on the board: read the three words, circle the letters they share, and write the root word. Read the words of the other cards aloud once.
script.stuck: Have the child cover the beginnings and the endings of the words with a finger until a small real word shows. The root word must be a word by itself. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the root words are cheer, use, play, act, power, joy, care, sleep, and rest.

blocks.title: Write About the Picture: What You See
blocks.instruction: Sentence starters help you begin. The word bank names everything.

script.say: "Look at the picture. You are going to write three sentences about it. The beginning of each sentence is already on the line. The word bank under the picture gives you the names of the animals."
script.first: Look at the picture together and read the word bank aloud. Say a sentence together for the first starter: "I can see a fox and a panda." Write it on the board. Tell the children to finish each sentence with their own words and to end it with a period.
script.stuck: Ask the child a question about the picture: "Which animals can you see? What is the panda doing? Which one do you like, and why?" Have the child say the sentence aloud before writing it. A child who finishes early writes one more sentence on the last lines.

blocks.title: Add It Again
blocks.instruction: Each ring holds the same amount. Finish the addition.

script.say: "The animals on this page stand in equal groups: every ring holds the same number. Count how many are in one ring. Then finish the addition and write how many there are in all."
script.first: Do the first one on the board. Ask, "How many rings? How many animals in each ring?" Read the addition aloud: "4 plus 4." Count all the animals to check and write 8 in the box. Say it one more way: "2 groups of 4 make 8."
script.stuck: Have the child touch each ring and say how many are in it, then add the numbers one after another: for four rings of 2, "2, 4, 6, 8." Counting every animal one by one is fine as a check. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 8, 8, 8, and 6.

blocks.title: Quarter Hours
blocks.instruction: Read each clock. Circle the matching time.

script.say: "Every clock on this page shows a quarter hour: something o'clock, quarter past, half past, or quarter to. Read each clock and circle the time that matches."
script.first: Draw a clock on the board. Show where the long hand points for each quarter hour: on the 12 for :00, on the 3 for :15, on the 6 for :30, and on the 9 for :45. Do the first clock on the page together: read the short hand for the hour first, then the long hand for the minutes.
script.stuck: Ask, "Which number has the short hand just passed?" That is the hour, even when the short hand is close to the next number. Then have the child count by fives from the 12 to the long hand: 5, 10, 15. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the clocks show 11:15, 1:45, 2:45, and 8:45.

blocks.title: Mirror Line?
blocks.instruction: Is the dashed line a mirror line? Circle the check or the cross.

script.say: "A mirror line cuts a picture into two halves that match exactly, like a picture and its reflection in a mirror. Look at the dashed line on each animal. If both sides match, circle the check. If they do not match, circle the cross."
script.first: Do the first two together. Ask about the first animal, "If we folded the picture on the dashed line, would one side land exactly on the other?" Have a child point to parts that match on both sides. For the second animal, ask what is on one side and missing on the other.
script.stuck: Have the child cover one side of the picture with a hand, look at the other side, and then switch. Ask, "Is there a wing here? Is there one on the other side, too?" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the bat and the sheep have a mirror line; the swan and the seagull do not.

blocks.title: Mirror Pictures: Heart and Butterfly
blocks.instruction: Each picture is only half done. Color the squares on the other side of the line to make it symmetrical.

script.say: "Each picture on this page is only half done. The dashed line is a mirror. Color squares on the empty side so that both sides match exactly."
script.first: Do the first row of the first picture together. Count how many squares are colored in that row, starting at the dashed line and counting away from it. Color the same number of squares on the other side, starting at the line again. Tell the children to work row by row from the top.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the dashed line in one row and count the colored squares away from the line, then count the same number on the other side. A square next to the line has its partner next to the line; a square far from the line has its partner just as far away.

packs.title: Second Grade Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Second Grade Emergency Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the end of the year in second grade: 8 review blocks in reading, word work, writing, and math, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Odd Number Hunt
blocks.instruction: Circle every ODD number. Look at the last digit to decide.

script.say: "Even numbers can be split into two equal groups. Odd numbers always have one left over. You only need to look at the last digit. If a number ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9, it is odd. Circle every odd number."
script.first: Write 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 on the board and leave it there. Do the first row together: for each number, point to the last digit and ask, "Is it on our list?" Circle the number if it is. Show with 12 that the first digit does not matter: the 1 is on our list, but 12 ends in 2, so 12 is not odd. Only the last digit counts.
script.stuck: Have the child cover every digit but the last one with a finger and check it against the list on the board. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the odd numbers are 63, 47, 93, 21, 37, 73, 87, and 43.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: Story 2
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. Then read each question and circle the best answer. The answers are in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, find the sentence in the story that answers it, and circle the answer. The children do the other questions on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask them to put a finger on the sentence in the story that tells the answer. If the child cannot read the story alone, read it with them. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are yellow, in the park, and the wind is strong.

blocks.title: Synonyms for Said: Pick the Word That Fits
blocks.instruction: Read each sentence and write the word from the bubble that fits best in the box instead of said.

script.say: "Writers do not use the word said over and over. They pick a word that tells how something was said. Read each sentence. Choose the word from the bubble that fits best, and write it in the box."
script.first: Read the six words in the bubble aloud together, and have the children say "Wait for me!" in a shout and then in a whisper. Do the first sentence together: try two or three of the words in the gap and ask which one fits someone running after a bus. Tell the children to cross out each word once they have used it; every word is used one time.
script.stuck: Read the sentence to the child and ask how the person would say it: loudly, quietly, as a question? Then read the words that are left in the bubble. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are shouted, whispered, asked, promised, explained, and answered.

blocks.title: Retell the Story with Starters
blocks.instruction: Write what happens in each picture on its lines, starting with the word printed on the first line.

script.say: "The four pictures tell a story from beginning to end. Write what happens in each picture on its lines. The first word is already there: First, Next, Then, Finally. The word bank at the top gives you words you may need."
script.first: Look at the four pictures together and have four children each tell what happens in one. Read the word bank aloud. Say a sentence for the first picture together and write it on the board: "First, the boy gets his paint and his brush." Tell the children to write one or two sentences for each picture and to end each one with a period.
script.stuck: Point to one picture and ask, "What is the boy doing here? What is different from the picture before?" Have the child say the sentence aloud, starting with the printed word, before writing it. A word that is spelled by its sounds is fine.

blocks.title: Fair Shares?
blocks.instruction: Circle every shape that is cut into EQUAL parts.

script.say: "Equal parts are parts that are exactly the same size. Look at each shape. If it is cut into equal parts, circle it. If some parts are bigger than others, leave it alone."
script.first: Draw two bars on the board: one cut into three parts of the same size, and one cut into a big part and two small parts. Ask, "In which bar would everyone get a fair share?" Circle that one. Do the first row of the page together the same way.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on one part and ask, "Is every other part just as big as this one?" If one part is clearly bigger or smaller, the shape is not circled. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the shapes with equal parts are the third shape in row 1, the first and the third in row 2, the second and the third in row 3, and the third in row 4.

blocks.title: Shopping Math: How Much Change?
blocks.instruction: Count the coins paid, then work out the change.

script.say: "At the top of the page is a shelf with five toy animals and their prices. Each question tells you what someone buys and shows the coins they pay with. Count the coins. Then figure out how much money they get back. That money is called the change."
script.first: Read the five prices on the shelf aloud together. Do the first question together: find the price of the animal Mia buys. Count her coins: two quarters are 50 cents. Ask, "She pays 50 cents, and the toy costs less than that. How much does she get back?" Count up from the price to 50, write the subtraction in the work space, and write the change in the box. The printed directions say "work out the change"; tell the children that means figure it out. The page has only two questions: a child who finishes picks another animal from the shelf and figures out the change from 50 cents on the back of the page.
script.stuck: Have the child write the price and count up to 50 by tens or fives, keeping track on fingers. Drawn dimes help: draw 50 cents as five dimes and cross out the price. For your own reference, on the page for everyone Mia buys the fox for 40 cents and gets 10 cents back, and Leo buys the giraffe for 30 cents and gets 20 cents back. For the other animals, the change from 50 cents is 30 cents (the 20-cent animal), 15 cents (the 35-cent animal), and 5 cents (the 45-cent animal).

blocks.title: Grid Coordinates: Write the Codes
blocks.instruction: The picture is colored in. Write the code of each square in the list for its color.

script.say: "This grid already has a picture colored in. Every square has a name made of a letter and a number, like B2. Write the name of each colored square in the list for its color."
script.first: Show how to name a square: go straight up from the square to its letter and straight to the side to its number, and write the letter first. Do the first colored square together and write its code in the first box of the list. Tell the children to put a small dot on each square once its code is written.
script.stuck: Have the child put one finger on the square and move it straight up to read the letter, then straight to the left to read the number. The order of the codes in the list does not matter, as long as every colored square is there once.

blocks.title: Dot-to-Dot: Count by Fives
blocks.instruction: Start at the orange dot. Count by fives from 5 to 50 and join the dots. Part of the picture is already drawn.

script.say: "This is a dot-to-dot, and you count by fives. Start at the orange dot at 5. Draw a line to 10, then to 15, and keep going to 50."
script.first: Count by fives from 5 to 50 aloud together. Find the orange dot at 5 together. Ask, "What comes after 5 when we count by fives?" Draw the first line together. The row of numbers at the bottom of the page shows the order.
script.stuck: Have the child say the number they are on and add five; that is the dot to look for. The numbers in the row at the bottom can be crossed off one by one.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the start of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Addition with Carrying
blocks.instruction: Add one place at a time. Regroup when you need to carry.

script.say: "These are addition problems, written one number under the other. Add one place at a time, starting with the ones. When a place adds up to ten or more, regroup: write the ones digit of that sum and carry the 1 to the next place."
script.first: Write the second problem on the board the way it is printed: 18 plus 55. Add the ones: 8 plus 5 is 13, so write 3 under the ones and carry the 1 into the small box above the tens. Add the tens: 1 plus 5 plus the carried 1 is 7. Read the whole answer aloud: 73. Tell the children that in some problems the tens add up to ten or more; then the answer has three digits.
script.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and say its sum aloud. If the sum is ten or more, ask, "Which digit stays here, and which digit is carried?" The child checks the small box before adding the next column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 149, 73, 123, 134, 117, and 54.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: Story 3
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentence in the story helps us decide. (The sentences are numbered.) Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child say the answer aloud first and start it with part of the question: "Ben needs his boot because …" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are happy and rainy; for question 3, any answer that says Ben wants to go out and play in the puddles is right.

blocks.title: Prefixes re-, pre- and mis-: Pick by Meaning
blocks.instruction: Read what each new word means, find its prefix in the key and write it in the empty piece.

script.say: "A prefix is a small part at the front of a word that changes its meaning. The key at the top shows three prefixes: re means again, pre means before, and mis means wrongly. Read what each new word means. Then write the right prefix in the empty piece in front of the word."
script.first: Read the key at the top aloud together. Do the first one together: "to fill an empty cup back up." Ask, "Is that again, before, or wrongly?" It is again, so the prefix is re. Write it in the empty piece and have the class read the new word aloud: refill.
script.stuck: Read the meaning to the child and ask for the clue: "one more time" or "back" points to re, "early," "first," or "ahead" points to pre, and "not right" or "lose" points to mis. Then the child says the new word aloud. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are refill, preview, misplace, prepay, reread, miscount, preheat, and misspell.

blocks.title: Write What Is Different
blocks.instruction: Circle the 3 differences (something may be gone), then write one sentence about each one on the lines, using the words in the two strips.

script.say: "Here are two pictures that look almost the same. Picture 2 is different in 3 places. Circle each difference in picture 2. Then write one sentence about each difference on the lines. The words in the two strips under the pictures help you."
script.first: Find one difference together and circle it in picture 2. Read the two strips aloud: the first strip names things in the picture, and the second strip tells how a thing can change. Build a sentence together and write it on the board, for example: "In picture 2, the sun is smaller." Show that every line already starts with "In picture 2," so the children only finish the sentence.
script.stuck: Have the child compare one small part of the two pictures at a time, from top to bottom. For the sentence, ask, "Which thing is it? What happened to it?" The child picks one word from each strip and says the sentence aloud before writing it. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the differences are in the sun, the clouds, and the elephant.

blocks.title: Shopping Math: Buying Three Things
blocks.instruction: Each basket holds three things. Add all three prices.

script.say: "At the top of the page is a shelf with five fruits and their prices. Each question shows three fruits that someone buys. Find the three prices on the shelf, add them, and write the total."
script.first: Read the five prices on the shelf aloud together. Do the first question together: find the three fruits on the shelf and write their three prices in the work space. Add two of the prices first, then add the third. Write the total in the box in front of the cent sign.
script.stuck: Have the child circle the three fruits on the shelf that the question shows and write the three prices one under the other. It helps to start with two prices that make an easy number, such as 40 and 10. Drawn dimes and nickels help a child who cannot add the numbers yet.

blocks.title: Count by Threes
blocks.instruction: Skip count by 3. Write each missing number.

script.say: "On this page we count by threes: 3, 6, 9, 12. Some numbers are missing. Count by threes and write each missing number. The rows do not start at 3."
script.first: Count by threes to 30 aloud together. Do the first row on the board: read the numbers that are there and ask, "How far is it from one number to the next?" Add three to the last number before the gap and write the answer in.
script.stuck: Have the child add three to the number before the gap with fingers: say the number, then count three more. To check, the next printed number must be three more than the number the child wrote. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the missing numbers are 48, 51, 54 in the first row; 21, 24, 27 in the second; 39, 42, 48 in the third; 36, 42, 45 in the fourth; and 33, 39, 45 in the fifth.

blocks.title: Mystery Number: Two Arrows, One Square
blocks.instruction: Follow both arrows. They point to the same square of the chart. Write the mystery number.

script.say: "Each puzzle has two numbers, and each number has an arrow. The key at the top tells what the arrows do: up is 10 less, down is 10 more, left is 1 less, and right is 1 more. Both arrows lead to the same number. Find that mystery number and write it in the box."
script.first: Point to the key at the top of the page and read it aloud together. The printed directions mention "the chart": that is a hundreds chart, where one square to the right is 1 more and one square down is 10 more. No chart is printed on the page, and none is needed. Do the first puzzle on the board: "24, arrow down: 10 more is 34. 33, arrow to the right: 1 more is 34." Both arrows land on 34, so 34 is the mystery number. Tell the children to follow both arrows every time; the second arrow checks the first.
script.stuck: Have the child say what the arrow does before using it, and follow only one arrow at first. Then the child follows the second arrow; if the two answers are not the same, one of them needs another look. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the mystery numbers are 34, 18, 51, 28, 63, 30, 50, and 26.

blocks.title: Mirror Pictures: House and Crown
blocks.instruction: Each picture is only half done. Color the squares on the other side of the line to make it symmetrical.

script.say: "Each picture on this page is only half done. The dashed line is a mirror. Color squares on the empty side so that both sides match exactly."
script.first: Do the first row of the first picture together. Count how many squares are colored in that row, starting at the dashed line and counting away from it. Color the same number of squares on the other side, starting at the line again. Tell the children to work row by row from the top.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the dashed line in one row and count the colored squares away from the line, then count the same number on the other side. A square next to the line has its partner next to the line; a square far from the line has its partner just as far away.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Start of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the start of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Where on the Number Line? 60 to 100
blocks.instruction: The line starts at sixty. Count on from the nearest printed number.

script.say: "These number lines do not start at zero. They start at 60 and go to 100. Each arrow points to a number. Find out which number it is and write it in the box."
script.first: Draw the first number line on the board. Read the printed numbers aloud: 60, 65, 70, and so on to 100. Ask, "How much is one small step?" (One.) Find the printed number closest to the first arrow and count on or back from it to the arrow.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the nearest printed number and count the small marks one by one to the arrow. An answer that is much too small means the child counted from the left end as if it were zero; point to the 60.

blocks.title: Read and Answer
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentences in the story help us decide. (The sentences are numbered.) Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child say the answer aloud first and start it with part of the question: "Emma checks the garden because …" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are "She takes good care of the plants" and "eat them"; for question 3, any answer that says a rabbit ate two carrots is right.

blocks.title: Synonym Pairs: Match the Words That Mean the Same
blocks.instruction: Draw a line to link each word on the left with the word on the right that means the same.

script.say: "Synonyms are words that mean the same thing, or almost the same, like big and large. Each word on the left has a partner on the right that means the same. Draw a line from each word to its partner."
script.first: Read the words in both columns aloud once, because some of them may be new to the children. Do the first one together: "yummy." Read down the right column and ask which word means the same. Draw a line from yummy to delicious. Tell the children to start with the pairs they are sure about; the last ones get easier.
script.stuck: Read the word to the child and have the child put it into a short sentence, such as "The soup is yummy." Then the child tries the words on the right in the same sentence. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the pairs are yummy and delicious, tumble and fall, speak and talk, scared and frightened, happy and cheerful, weep and cry, hushed and quiet, cluttered and messy.

blocks.title: Verb Forms: Today and Yesterday
blocks.instruction: Look at the picture and read the verb. Write its today form and its yesterday form in the dashed boxes, then finish the sentences.

script.say: "A verb changes its form. For something he or she does today, most verbs get an s: jumps. For something that happened yesterday, the verb changes again: jumped. Fill in the missing forms in the chart. Then finish the three sentences under it."
script.first: Look at the chart together: the verb, its form for he or she today, and its form for yesterday. Do the row for "dance" together by saying two sentences: "Today she dances. Yesterday she danced." Write "dances" in the empty box. Tell the children that some verbs do not add -ed for yesterday; they say the sentence aloud and listen for what sounds right.
script.stuck: Have the child say two sentences aloud for the verb: "Today he ___. Yesterday he ___." For your own reference, on the page for everyone the forms are dances and danced, reads and read, jumps and jumped, wanders and wandered, runs and ran, sings and sang; the three sentences take danced, sang, and reads.

blocks.title: Subtraction with Borrowing
blocks.instruction: Subtract one place at a time. Regroup when you need to borrow.

script.say: "These are subtraction problems, written one number under the other. Subtract one place at a time, starting with the ones. When the top digit is too small, regroup: take one ten from the tens place and turn it into ten ones."
script.first: Write the first problem on the board the way it is printed: 73 minus 17. Look at the ones: "3 minus 7. Can we do that?" No, so regroup: cross out the 7 tens and write 6, and turn the 3 ones into 13. Now 13 minus 7 is 6, and 6 tens minus 1 ten is 5 tens. Read the whole answer aloud: 56.
script.stuck: Have the child ask at the ones place, "Is the top digit big enough?" If not, the child crosses out the tens digit, writes one less above it, and puts a small 1 in front of the ones digit. The most common slip is to subtract the smaller digit from the bigger one no matter which is on top. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 56, 37, 19, 36, 27, and 48.

blocks.title: Read the Calendar: A Busy Month
blocks.instruction: Find the date one week later, and count the days from one sticker to another.

script.say: "This is a calendar page for one month. Some days have a little picture on them, like a sticker. The questions ask you to find dates, to go one week ahead, and to count the days from one sticker to another."
script.first: Read the name of the month and the names of the days across the top together. Do the first question together: find the date, put a finger on it, and go straight up to the name of the day. Then show what one week later means: one row straight down, which is 7 days.
script.stuck: For a day of the week, have the child find the date and move a finger straight up its column. To count the days from one sticker to another, the child starts on the day after the first sticker and counts every day up to and including the second sticker. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are Friday, 4, the 9th, the 17th, and 21.

blocks.title: Parts of a Plant and Their Functions
blocks.instruction: Read what each part does. Find that part on the plant and write the number of its tag in the box.

script.say: "This is a science page about the parts of a plant. The plant in the picture has five tags with numbers. Next to it are five sentences. Each sentence tells what one part of the plant does. Find that part on the plant and write the number of its tag in the box."
script.first: Point to each tag on the plant and name the parts together: the flower, a leaf, the stem, the seeds in their pod, and the roots. Do one sentence together: "takes in water from the soil." Ask, "Which part of the plant is down in the soil?" The roots; write the number of their tag in the box.
script.stuck: Read the sentence to the child and ask a question about it: "Which part is flat and green and faces the sun? Which part do bees visit? Which part is like a straw that holds everything up?" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are, from top to bottom, 2 (seeds), 4 (leaf), 5 (roots), 1 (stem), and 3 (flower).

blocks.title: Grid Coordinates on a 6x6 Grid
blocks.instruction: Find each square by its letter and number. Color it to reveal the picture.

script.say: "This grid hides a picture. Every square has a name made of a letter and a number, like B2. The lists at the bottom tell you which squares to color and in which color."
script.first: Make sure every child has the crayons the lists name. Show how to find a square: put one finger on the letter at the top and one finger on the number at the side, and move them until they meet. Find the first square of the first list together and color it. Tell the children to cross out each code once its square is colored.
script.stuck: Have the child say the code aloud, letter first, then find the letter's column and slide a finger down to the number's row. A square in the wrong place shows in the picture; the child can check its code again.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the middle of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Pick the Array
blocks.instruction: Circle the array that matches the multiplication.

script.say: "An array is a set of things in rows, with the same number in every row. Each problem shows a multiplication and three arrays. Circle the array that matches the multiplication."
script.first: Do the first one together. Read "3 × 4" aloud as "3 rows of 4." On this page the times sign means "rows of." Look at each of the three arrays: count its rows, then count how many are in one row. Circle the array with 3 rows and 4 in each row. Count all the things in it to check: there are 12.
script.stuck: Have the child run a finger along each row of an array and count the rows first, then count the things in the top row. On this page the first number is the number of rows and the second number is how many are in each row.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: Story 2
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence. When you finish, turn the page over and write three sentences that tell what happens next in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentence in the story helps us decide. (The sentences are numbered.) Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child find the sentence about the boy and say the answer aloud before writing it. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are "happy and proud" and "a windy day"; for question 3, the boy claps and says the kite looks like a little dragon.

blocks.title: Word Fields: Words for Go and Look
blocks.instruction: Write each word in the field it belongs to.

script.say: "Some words belong together because they are about the same thing. The ten words at the top are all ways to go or ways to look. Write each word in the field where it belongs: the field for go or the field for look."
script.first: Read the ten words aloud together. Act out two of them: ask a volunteer to creep across the front of the room, and have everyone squint. Ask, "Is creeping a way to go or a way to look?" Write creep in the field for go. Tell the children to cross out each word at the top once it is written in a field.
script.stuck: Read the word to the child and have the child try it in two sentences: "I ___ across the room" and "I ___ at the picture." The sentence that makes sense tells the field. Observe and watch do not fit either sentence; for those two, try "I ___ the birds," which is a way to look. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words for go are creep, stroll, hurry, and walk; the words for look are squint, gaze, peek, glance, observe, and watch.

blocks.title: Write About the Picture: Your Own Words
blocks.instruction: No sentence starters this time. Use the word bank and write your own story.

script.say: "Look at the picture of the fruit. You are going to write your own sentences about it. There are no sentence starters this time. The word bank under the picture gives you the names of the fruits."
script.first: Look at the picture together and read the word bank aloud; some of the names, such as persimmon and nectarine, may be new. Collect ideas aloud: Which fruit is the biggest in the picture? What colors can you see? Which one would you like to taste? Write one sentence on the board as an example: "The lime is bigger than the pineapple in this picture." Tell the children to write at least four sentences and to end each one with a period.
script.stuck: Ask the child a question about the picture: "Which fruit would you pick? What color is it? What could you make with it?" Have the child say the sentence aloud before writing it. The names of the fruits are copied from the word bank. A child who finishes early turns the sentences into a short story on the back of the page.

blocks.title: Times Tables Practice
blocks.instruction: Multiply. Write each product in the box.

script.say: "This is multiplication practice with facts from different times tables. Multiply, and write each product in the box. Do the facts you know by heart first. Then go back and figure out the others."
script.first: Do the first two facts on the board. For 6 times 3, ask the children how they know the answer: by heart, by counting by threes six times, or by turning the fact around to 3 times 6. Accept every way that gives the right answer.
script.stuck: Have the child turn the fact around if that is easier, count by the smaller number on fingers, or start from a fact the child knows: 5 times 7 is 35, and two more sevens make 49. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the products are 18, 42, 21, 27, 10, 6, 14, 40, 49, 16, 15, and 32.

blocks.title: Multiplication Word Problems
blocks.instruction: The picture shows the equal groups. Write each answer in the box.

script.say: "These are multiplication word problems. Each story tells about equal groups, and the picture under the story shows them. Read the story, write the multiplication in the work space, and write the answer in the box."
script.first: Read the first story aloud together. Ask, "How many rows are there? How many swans are in each row?" Write the multiplication on the board: 3 times 2 equals 6. Count the swans in the picture to check. Have the children write the answer as a sentence on the lines: "There are 6 swans altogether."
script.stuck: Ask the child to underline the two numbers in the story and to say what each number counts: the groups, or how many are in each group. The picture shows the groups, and counting them is fine as a check. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 6 swans and 16 zebras.

blocks.title: How Animals Adapt
blocks.instruction: Write the letter of the animal each sentence tells about in its box; one animal is left over.

script.say: "This is a science page about how animals are built for the way they live. At the top are seven animals, each with a letter. Each sentence tells about one of them. Read the sentence, decide which animal it is, and write that animal's letter in the box. One animal is left over."
script.first: Name the seven animals together and say their letters. Read the first sentence aloud together: "Its wings are flippers: it swims fast but cannot fly." Ask, "Which animal has wings and cannot fly?" Write its letter in the box. Tell the children to cross out each animal once they have used it.
script.stuck: Read the sentence to the child and ask for the body part it names: teeth, a trunk, a beak, a hump. Then the child looks for that body part in the pictures. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the letters are, from top to bottom, G (penguin), B (beaver), A (elephant), F (toucan), E (woodpecker), and C (camel); the monkey is left over.

blocks.title: Big Picture Sudoku
blocks.instruction: Every row, column, and box needs all six pictures — fill the empty cells.

script.say: "This is a picture sudoku with six animals. Every row, every column, and every box with a thick border needs all six animals, each one exactly one time. Draw the missing animals in the empty cells. A quick sketch is enough."
script.first: Hold up the page and show a row, a column, and one of the boxes with a thick border. Find a row or a box together that has only one or two empty cells. Ask, "Which animals are already here? Which ones are missing?" If two are missing, look up and down the column of an empty cell to see which of the two is already there. Fill in one cell together. Tell the children that this puzzle takes time and that it is fine if they do not finish it today.
script.stuck: Have the child choose the row, column, or box with the fewest empty cells and go through the six animals in the strip at the bottom one by one, pointing to each one that is already there. To check a finished row or column, the child runs a finger along it: no animal may be there twice.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: Middle of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the middle of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Crack the Pattern
blocks.instruction: Find each row’s rule. Write the missing numbers.

script.say: "Each row of numbers follows a rule: the numbers go up by the same amount every time. Find the rule of the row. Then write the missing numbers."
script.first: Write the first row on the board the way it is printed. Find two numbers that stand side by side with no gap between them: 108 and 114. Ask, "How far is it from 108 to 114?" Six. Check the rule with 84 and 96: that is two steps of six. Fill in the missing numbers by adding six each time. Tell the children to find the rule of every row the same way.
script.stuck: Have the child find two numbers that stand next to each other with no gap and count up from one to the other. Where there is one empty box between two numbers, the jump is two steps: in the second row, from 48 to 60 is 12, so one step is 6. The child checks by counting on along the whole row. For your own reference, every row on the page for everyone goes up by 6.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: The Tallest Sunflower
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence. When you finish, turn the page over and write three sentences that tell what happens next in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentences in the story help us decide. (The sentences are numbered.) Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child say the answer aloud first and start it with part of the question: "Owen takes a photo because …" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are "the plants grow very tall" and "proud"; for question 3, Owen wants to show the photo to his class.

blocks.title: Root Words in Sentences
blocks.instruction: Write the four words above each stone into the sentences below it, one word in each gap.

script.say: "The four words above each stone are a word family: they are all built from the root word on the stone. Each word fits into one of the four sentences below it. Read each sentence and write the word that fits in the gap. Use every word one time."
script.first: Read the four words of the first family aloud together: enjoy, enjoyment, joyful, joyfully. Point to their root word, joy. Do the first sentence together by trying the words in the gap: "The dog jumped enjoy when we came home? The dog jumped joyfully when we came home." Tell the children to cross out each word once they have used it.
script.stuck: Read the sentence to the child once with each of the words that are left and ask which one sounds right. The child starts with the sentences they are sure about; the last word goes in the last gap. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are, in order, joyfully, enjoy, enjoyment, joyful, then sleeper, sleepy, sleepiness, sleepily.

blocks.title: Ask About the Picture: Why and How
blocks.instruction: Look at the picture. Finish each question. Start with the word already on the line.

script.say: "Look at the four pictures at the top of the page. You are going to ask questions about them. Each line already starts with a question word: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How. Finish each question, and end it with a question mark."
script.first: Name the four pictures together: a builder, a pear, a house, and a clock. Make up a question for the first line aloud and write it on the board with its question mark: "Who builds the house?" Ask two children for a question that starts with What. Tell the class that any question that fits one of the pictures and starts with the printed word is right, and that nobody has to answer the questions.
script.stuck: Point to one picture and ask the child what they would like to know about it. Then help the child say it as a question that starts with the printed word, for example: "Where does the builder work? When does the clock ring? Why is the pear red and yellow? How tall is the house?"

blocks.title: 3-Digit Addition with Carrying
blocks.instruction: Add one place at a time. Regroup when you need to carry.

script.say: "These are addition problems with three-digit numbers, written one number under the other. Add one place at a time, starting with the ones. When a place adds up to ten or more, regroup: write the ones digit of that sum and carry the 1 to the next place."
script.first: Write the first problem on the board the way it is printed: 261 plus 285. Add the ones: 1 plus 5 is 6. Add the tens: 6 plus 8 is 14, so write 4 under the tens and carry the 1 into the small box above the hundreds. Add the hundreds: 2 plus 2 plus the carried 1 is 5. Read the whole answer aloud: 546. Point out that the small boxes above each problem are for the carried digits.
script.stuck: Have the child cover all but one column and say its sum aloud. If the sum is ten or more, ask, "Which digit stays here, and which digit is carried?" The most common slip is to forget the carried 1; the child checks the small box before adding the next column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 546, 521, 708, 909, 889, and 703.

blocks.title: Times Families
blocks.instruction: Use the array to finish all four number sentences.

script.say: "Multiplication and division belong together. One array gives a whole family of four facts: two multiplications and two divisions. Use each array to finish all four number sentences next to it."
script.first: Draw the first array on the board: 2 rows of 5. Count the rows and count how many are in one row. Finish the two multiplications: 2 times 5 is 10, and 5 times 2 is 10. Then ask, "Ten shapes in 2 equal rows: how many are in each row?" Finish the two divisions: 10 divided by 2 is 5, and 10 divided by 5 is 2. Show that all four facts use the same three numbers.
script.stuck: Have the child count the rows, the shapes in one row, and all the shapes, and write these three numbers next to the array. Every number sentence of the family uses only these three numbers. For a division, ask, "How many groups of 5 can you see in the array?" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the four arrays hold 10, 30, 15, and 12 shapes.

blocks.title: Magic Squares
blocks.instruction: Every row and column adds up to the magic number. Fill the empty cells.

script.say: "In a magic square, every row and every column adds up to the same number: the magic number. On this page the magic number is 15. Fill in the empty cells so that every row and every column adds up to 15."
script.first: Draw the first square on the board. Find a row or a column with only one empty cell: the top row has 6 and 1. Ask, "6 and 1 make 7. How many more do we need to get to 15?" Write 8 in the empty cell. Tell the children to look for a row or a column with just one empty cell each time; every number they fill in opens up the next one.
script.stuck: Have the child run a finger along a row or a column with one empty cell, add the two numbers that are there, and count up to 15. To check a finished square, the child adds every row and every column. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the rows of the first square are 6, 1, 8, then 7, 5, 3, then 2, 9, 4; the rows of the second square are 6, 7, 2, then 1, 5, 9, then 8, 3, 4.

blocks.title: Mirror Below the Line
blocks.instruction: The pictures lie on their side. Each one is only half done: color the squares below the line to make it symmetrical.

script.say: "Each picture on this page is only half done, and it lies on its side. The dashed line is a mirror. Color squares below the line so that the bottom half matches the top half exactly."
script.first: Do the first column of the first picture together. Count how many squares are colored in that column, starting at the dashed line and counting up. Color the same number of squares below the line, starting at the line again and counting down. Tell the children to work column by column from the left.
script.stuck: Have the child put a finger on the dashed line in one column and count the colored squares going up, then count the same number going down. A square that touches the line has its partner touching the line; a square far from the line has its partner just as far away.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 1
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the end of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Number Machines
blocks.instruction: Each machine uses its rule on every number. Fill in the missing ones.

script.say: "Each number machine has a rule, printed at the top. A number goes in on the left, the machine uses its rule, and a new number comes out on the right. One machine multiplies, and one subtracts. Fill in the missing numbers. Watch out: sometimes the number that went in is the one that is missing."
script.first: Do the first machine together. Its rule is times 5. Ask, "6 goes in. What comes out?" Write 30. Then do the row where the box on the left is empty: "Something went in, the machine multiplied it by 5, and 35 came out. What went in?" Work backward: 35 divided by 5 is 7. Check it by putting 7 through the machine.
script.stuck: Ask the child, "Is the missing number before the arrow or after it?" After the arrow, the child uses the rule. Before the arrow, the child does the opposite (divide for times, add for minus) and then checks by putting the number through the machine. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the first machine gives 30, 60, 7, 50, and 2; the second gives 18, 15, 7, 27, and 9.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: Story 5
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence. When you finish, turn the page over and write three sentences that tell what happens next in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. The story says the children cannot go out for "break" and that the teacher opens the game "cupboard"; tell the class that this means recess and a cabinet. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentences in the story help us decide. Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child say the answer aloud first and start it with part of the question: "The teacher opens the game cupboard because …" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are "they are having fun" and "that they were no fun"; for question 3, any answer that says the children cannot go outside because of the rain is right.

blocks.title: Who Does It? The Person Word
blocks.instruction: Look at each person, read the word beside them and write the person word in the empty brick.

script.say: "Many words for people are made from a verb and an ending. Someone who teaches is a teacher. Look at each person, read the word next to them, and write the word for the person who does it in the empty brick."
script.first: Do the first two on the board. Ask, "Someone who runs is a …?" Write runner and point out the double n. Ask, "Someone who takes photographs is a …?" Write photographer. Tell the children that every person word on this page ends in -er.
