script.stuck: Have the child say the sentence aloud: "Someone who ___ is a ___." For the spelling: a word that ends in e only adds an r, as in dance and dancer; run doubles its last letter. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the words are runner, photographer, dancer, gardener, teacher, baker, farmer, and singer.

blocks.title: Compare Two Animals: Same and Different
blocks.instruction: Read both fact files. For each fact, circle same or different. Then write two things that are the same and two that are different.

script.say: "Here are two fact files, one for a ladybug and one for an eagle. Each file gives four facts about its animal. Compare the facts one by one and circle same or different. Then write two things that are the same and two things that are different."
script.first: Read both fact files aloud together. Do the first fact together: "Animal group: the ladybug is an insect, and the eagle is a bird. Same or different?" Circle different. Write a sentence for it on the board: "Different: A ladybug is an insect, but an eagle is a bird." Tell the children to write whole sentences on the lines. The fact files use short words: "air" means that the animal flies, and "meat" means that it eats other animals (a ladybug eats tiny insects). If a child questions a fact, say that the job is to compare what the two files say.
script.stuck: Have the child put one finger on a fact in the ladybug's file and one finger on the same line in the eagle's file and read both aloud. For the sentences, give the child a frame: "Both animals ___." and "The ladybug ___, but the eagle ___." For your own reference, on the page for everyone the animal group and the body covering are different; where the animals live and what they eat are the same.

blocks.title: Count the Squares
blocks.instruction: Count the squares in the rectangle. Finish the multiplication.

script.say: "Each rectangle on this page is made of squares. The number of squares is the area of the rectangle. Count the rows, and count how many squares are in one row. Then finish the multiplication to find how many squares there are in all."
script.first: Draw the first rectangle on the board: 3 rows of 5 squares. Count the rows, then count the squares in one row. Say, "3 rows of 5: 3 times 5 is 15." Count the squares one by one to check. Say the answer as a sentence: "The area is 15 squares."
script.stuck: Have the child run a finger down the left side to count the rows and along the top to count the squares in one row. A child who does not know the fact adds the rows, 5 plus 5 plus 5, or counts every square. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 15, 16, 20, and 27.

blocks.title: Division Word Problems: Sharing
blocks.instruction: Each story shares things out. Deal them into the boxes.

script.say: "These are division word problems about sharing. Read each story. Decide how many things there are and how many equal groups they go into. Write the division, and write the answer in the box. The picture is there if you want to check."
script.first: Read the first story aloud together: 5 children share 30 pens. Ask, "How many pens in all? How many children?" Write the division on the board: 30 divided by 5. Ask how the children can find the answer: by knowing that 5 times 6 is 30, or by dealing the pens into the five boxes. Write 6 in the answer box, and write the whole division, with its answer, on the lines. Then say the answer together in a whole sentence: "Each child gets 6 pens."
script.stuck: Have the child underline the two numbers in the story and say what each one counts. Then ask for the multiplication fact: "4 times what makes 24?" A child who does not know the fact deals the things into the boxes with dots, one for each box in turn. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 6 pens, 6 notebooks, and 4 rulers.

blocks.title: The Water Cycle: Label the Diagram
blocks.instruction: Read the four words in the bank and write each one on the line that has the same number as on the diagram.

script.say: "This is a science page about the water cycle: the way water travels from the sea up into the sky and back down again. The diagram has four numbers. Read the four words in the bank, and write each word on the line that has the same number as its place in the diagram."
script.first: Follow the arrows in the diagram together, starting at the sea: the Sun warms the water and it rises into the air; high up it cools and forms a cloud; it falls as rain; it runs back to the sea. Read the four words aloud and say each one in plain words: evaporation means water rises into the air, condensation means it turns into the tiny drops of a cloud, precipitation means rain or snow falls, and collection means the water gathers in rivers, lakes, and the sea. Do number 1 together.
script.stuck: Point to the number in the diagram and ask, "What is the water doing here: going up, making a cloud, falling, or gathering?" Then read the four words to the child again. For your own reference, on the page for everyone 1 is evaporation, 2 is condensation, 3 is precipitation, and 4 is collection.

blocks.title: Grid Coordinates on a 10x10 Grid
blocks.instruction: Find each square on the big grid by its letter and number. Color it to reveal the picture.

script.say: "This grid hides a picture. Every square has a name made of a letter and a number, like B2. The lists at the bottom tell you which squares to color and in which color."
script.first: Make sure every child has the crayons the lists name. Show how to find a square: put one finger on the letter at the top and one finger on the number at the side, and move them until they meet. Find the first square of the first list together and color it. Tell the children to cross out each code once its square is colored.
script.stuck: Have the child say the code aloud, letter first, then find the letter's column and slide a finger down to the number's row. A square in the wrong place shows in the picture; the child can check its code again.

packs.title: Third Grade Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaTitle: Third Grade Emergency Sub Plans: End of the Year, Day 2
packs.metaDescription: No-prep emergency sub plans for the end of the year in third grade: 8 review blocks in reading, writing, math, and science, with a script for the guest teacher.

blocks.title: Rounding to the Nearest 10 and 100
blocks.instruction: Round each number twice: to the nearest ten in the first box and to the nearest hundred in the second.

script.say: "Rounding means finding the nearest round number. On this page you round each number two times: first to the nearest ten, then to the nearest hundred. The box at the top shows how: look at the digit to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4, round down. If it is 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9, round up."
script.first: Read the example at the top together: 472 is about 470 to the nearest ten, and about 500 to the nearest hundred. The wavy equal sign means "is about." Do the first number on the board. For the nearest ten, underline the tens digit of 159 and look at the ones digit: it is 9, so round up to 160. For the nearest hundred, underline the hundreds digit and look at the tens digit: it is 5, so round up to 200. Tell the children to start from the number on the page both times.
script.stuck: Have the child say the two tens the number is between (150 and 160) and ask which one is closer; then the two hundreds (100 and 200). A 5 always rounds up. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are 160 and 200; 490 and 500; 790 and 800; 310 and 300; 350 and 400; 540 and 500; 570 and 600; 560 and 600.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: Story 6
blocks.instruction: Read the story carefully. Then circle the best answer to each question.

script.say: "Now it is time to read. Read the story carefully, all the way to the end. You will not find the answers to questions 1 and 2 word for word in the story: look for clues and think about what the story tells you. Circle the best answer to questions 1 and 2. Then write your answer to question 3 on the lines, in a whole sentence. When you finish, turn the page over and write three sentences that tell what happens next in the story."
script.first: Have the children read the story quietly to themselves, then read it aloud once to the class. Do the first question together: read it, and ask which sentence in the story helps us decide. (The sentences are numbered.) Circle the answer. The children do the second question and the written answer on their own.
script.stuck: Read the question to the child and ask, "Which sentence in the story gives you a clue?" For the written answer, have the child say the answer aloud first and start it with part of the question: "Ella wants to surprise Grandpa because …" For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are "a little nervous" and "Ella practiced all week"; for question 3, any answer that says it is Grandpa's birthday, or that he is turning seventy, is right.

blocks.title: Root Words: Sort by the Root
blocks.instruction: Read each word at the top and write it on a line of the wall that stands on its root word.

script.say: "The twelve words at the top come from three word families. Each family is built from one root word: joy, thought, or worth. Read each word, find the root word inside it, and write the word on a line of the wall that stands on its root word."
script.first: Read the twelve words aloud together. Do two words together: "enjoyment." Ask, "Which root word is inside it?" Write it on a line above joy. Then do "afterthought" the same way. Tell the children to cross out each word at the top once it is written on a wall; each wall gets four words.
script.stuck: Have the child look for the letters of joy, thought, or worth inside the word and underline them. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the joy wall gets joyless, enjoyment, joyous, and enjoyable; the thought wall gets thoughtless, thoughtful, afterthought, and thoughtfully; the worth wall gets worthwhile, worthlessness, worthlessly, and worthy.

blocks.title: Retell the Story with Starters
blocks.instruction: Write what happens in each picture on its lines, starting with the word printed on the first line.

script.say: "The four pictures tell a story from beginning to end. Write what happens in each picture on its lines. Use words that show the order, such as first, next, then, and finally. The box at the top gives you words you may need."
script.first: Look at the four pictures together and ask four volunteers to tell what happens in one picture each. Read the words in the box aloud. This page has no sentence starters, even though its title says "with Starters"; the order words do that job. Write First, Next, Then, Finally on the board. Say a sentence for the first picture together and write it on the board: "First, a whole banana stands on a plate." Tell the children to write two sentences for each picture and to end each one with a period. A child who finishes early writes one more sentence on the back of the page: who ate the banana?
script.stuck: Point to one picture and ask, "What is different from the picture before?" Have the child say the sentence aloud, starting with one of the order words on the board, before writing it. A word that is spelled by its sounds is fine.

blocks.title: Name That Fraction
blocks.instruction: Write the fraction the shaded parts show.

script.say: "Each shape on this page is cut into equal parts, and some of the parts are shaded. Write the fraction that the shaded parts show. The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole shape has. The top number tells how many of them are shaded."
script.first: Draw the first shape on the board: a bar cut into four equal parts, with two of them shaded. Ask, "How many equal parts does the bar have in all?" Write 4 in the bottom box. Ask, "How many parts are shaded?" Write 2 in the top box. Read the fraction aloud: two fourths.
script.stuck: Have the child count all the parts first, shaded or not, and write that number at the bottom; then the child counts only the shaded parts for the top. The most common slip is to count only the parts that are not shaded for the bottom number.

blocks.title: Walk the Edge
blocks.instruction: Count the unit edges around each rectangle. Write the perimeter.

script.say: "The perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, like a walk along its edge. Each rectangle on this page is made of squares. Count the edges of the small squares all the way around the outside of the rectangle. Write the perimeter in the box."
script.first: Draw the first rectangle on the board. Mark a starting corner with a dot. Count the edges along the top, down the side, along the bottom, and back up to the dot, making a small mark on each edge as you count it. Write the total in the box. Then show the shortcut: count each of the four sides and add the four numbers.
script.stuck: Have the child mark a starting corner and make a small mark on each edge as it is counted, so that no edge is skipped or counted twice. A child who counts the squares inside is finding the area; point to the outside edge. A square in a corner has two outside edges, and both count. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the perimeters are 20, 14, 20, and 22.

blocks.title: Butterfly and Frog Life Cycles Compared
blocks.instruction: Read each sentence and put a check under the butterfly, the frog or both when it is true for that animal.

script.say: "This is a science page about two animals that change a great deal as they grow: the butterfly and the frog. Read each sentence. If it is true for the butterfly, put a check under the butterfly. If it is true for the frog, put a check under the frog. If it is true for both, check both."
script.first: Ask the children how each animal grows, and write the two chains on the board: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly; and egg, tadpole, young frog, frog. Do the first sentence together: "The grown-up catches insects to eat." That is true for the frog only, so only the frog gets a check. Tell the children that some sentences are true for both animals.
script.stuck: Read the sentence to the child and ask about each animal separately: "Is that true for the butterfly? Is it true for the frog?" Point to the two chains on the board. For your own reference, on the page for everyone the answers are, from top to bottom: frog, butterfly, both, frog, butterfly, frog, both, butterfly.

blocks.title: Bring the Crane Its Number
blocks.instruction: Start with the truck's number and, on your road, write the new number in each sign's box. Find the road that ends on the crane's number.

script.say: "The truck has to bring a number to the crane. The truck starts with 46, and the crane needs 54. There are several roads. Every sign on a road changes the number: plus 1, minus 10, and so on. Find the road that ends on the crane's number."
script.first: Hold up the page and show the truck with its number, the crane with its number, and one sign. Follow one road for two signs together and write the new number in the box of each sign: "46 plus 1 is 47." Tell the children to choose one road, write the new number in every box along it, and try another road if the last number is not 54.
script.stuck: Have the child write the new number in each sign's box before going on to the next sign. If a road ends on the wrong number, the child checks each step on that road first and then tries another road. Scrap paper is fine for the steps.
